opus-5.5.text:
I think compute is the bottleneck because so much of what we want to do in scientific AI is limited not by ideas but by our ability to test them at scale. In my work on AI for science, things like neural operators for weather forecasting, fluid dynamics, materials, and drug design, the data comes from physics. Often it comes from expensive numerical simulations, and generating that training data takes enormous compute in itself. Then you train models that have to capture phenomena across many scales, from the very fine to the very coarse, and that's also very compute hungry.

What's frustrating is that in academia especially, there's a huge gap between what a small group of large companies can do and what researchers at universities can do. Many important problems, like climate modeling, designing better catalysts, or understanding plasma in fusion reactors, are not the most commercially attractive in the short term, so they don't get the massive compute budgets. Yet these are exactly the areas where AI could have transformative impact on society.

We saw this with FourCastNet. Once we had access to enough GPUs, we could train a model that was tens of thousands of times faster than traditional weather models while staying competitive on accuracy. That opens up things like large ensembles for predicting extreme weather events, which simply weren't feasible before. Every time we've been able to scale up, we've learned something new about what these models can do.

So if I could remove one bottleneck, it would be compute. Democratizing access would let many more researchers explore these ideas, validate them rigorously, and bring them into the real world. Algorithms and data matter enormously too, but compute is what unlocks the experimentation loop that makes progress possible.

r001.rationale: The response says access to compute enables researchers to test ideas at scale, validate them, and explore what models can do.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I actually wouldn't pick compute as the bottleneck I'd remove, at least not in the naive sense of "give everyone more GPUs." I think the real bottleneck in the fields I care about, which is AI for science, is the gap between what the compute is being used for and what it could be used for.

Let me explain what I mean. Right now the dominant paradigm is to scale up transformers on internet text. That's wonderful for language, but the problems I work on, things like weather and climate modeling, fluid dynamics, designing medical devices like catheters, protein engineering, these are governed by physics. They live in continuous spaces, in function spaces, not in discrete tokens. And the data isn't lying around on the internet. You get it from expensive simulations or expensive experiments.

So if you just handed me ten times the compute and said "go," the first thing I'd do is not train a bigger language model. I'd generate data. I'd run the numerical solvers, the PDE solvers, at high resolution, across many regimes, and I'd use that to train neural operators that learn the underlying physics. That's what we did with FourCastNet, learning to forecast weather tens of thousands of times faster than numerical weather prediction, and the limiting factor there was never a shortage of GPUs for training. It was having enough high-quality simulated and observed data, and having architectures that actually respect the structure of the problem, resolution invariance, conservation laws, and so on.

There's also a cultural piece. Compute in academia is genuinely scarce, and that pushes students toward incremental work on small benchmarks instead of ambitious problems. So in that sense, yes, access matters, because it determines who gets to ask big questions. But if you remove only that bottleneck, you'll just see more people reproducing what industry is doing at smaller scale.

What I'd really want to remove is the bottleneck on the feedback loop between AI and the physical world. Simulation, experiment, prediction, and then back to a better model. Compute is one input into that loop, but so are open datasets, so are the right abstractions, and so is willingness to work across disciplines. If you fix the loop, the compute gets used wisely. If you only add compute, you mostly get bigger versions of what we already have.

r001.rationale: The response says compute access matters in academia because it determines who can pursue big research questions, and describes using compute to run high-resolution numerical solvers for research data.

astra-6.text:
I would choose compute because it determines how quickly we can turn ideas into experiments. You can have a promising new algorithm, but if you can’t test it at the right scale, it’s hard to understand what it can really do. More access lets us explore more ideas, learn from failures, and iterate faster.

That’s especially important in AI for science, where we want to model complex physical systems. Compute goes into generating training data, training the models, and validating their predictions. Relieving that bottleneck would let us tackle more ambitious problems—and let more researchers contribute, rather than limiting those experiments to a few well-resourced organizations.

r001.rationale: The response says access to more compute lets researchers test ideas at scale and conduct more experiments, identifying compute access as necessary for research experiments.

sol-6.1.text:
Because compute determines how quickly we can turn an idea into an experiment and learn from it. In AI, you can have a promising algorithm, but if you can’t test it at the right scale, it’s hard to know whether it really works. And when only a few organizations have access to that scale, we’re limiting who gets to contribute ideas.

For scientific AI, that’s especially important. We want to model complex physical systems, explore different conditions, and understand where our models are reliable. That takes substantial computation, both to generate data and to train and evaluate models. More accessible compute would let more researchers tackle those problems and iterate faster. It doesn’t replace good ideas, but it gives those ideas a chance to be tested.

r001.rationale: The response says compute is needed to turn ideas into experiments and test promising algorithms at the right scale, identifying access to compute as a prerequisite for research experiments.
